title: TCP Use-After-Free: CVE-2026-98432 / CVSS 9.8
author: oger
relevanceReason: 命中 6 个 AI/科技关键词。
summaryRaw: Trevor Fannin@trevorfanninFounder, AtlasSecurity alerts and CVE breakdowns, plus infrastructure and general tech.Followon X (opens in a new tab) #Overview Linux's stable kernels shipped a fix on October 11 and 15, 2026 for CVE-2026-98432, a use-after-free in the IPv4 TCP handshake that a remote, unauthenticated peer can reach. The kernel's own CVE Numbering Authority (CNA) scores it CVSS 3.1 9.8, Critical. The fixed releases are 5.10.272, 5.15.223, 6.1.190, 6.6.159, 6.12.113, 6.18.56, 7.2.10, and 7.3, and the bug goes back to Linux 4.4. The upstream fix is a four-line change, but most servers run a distribution's kernel. Red Hat, which now rates the bug Critical too, shipped fixed kernels for Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8, 9, and 10 on November 1, and AlmaLinux followed on November 2. Ubuntu has shipped a fixed kernel only for 26.10: as of 3:15 PM CST on November 3, its fixes for 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04 are still in testing, and its tracker reads "Vulnerable" for every release, 26.10 included.

Why it's urgent: the bug sits in code every Linux server runs when it accepts an IPv4 TCP connection, before any application sees the connection. Anthropic, whose researcher reported it, says its Claude model wrote a working proof-of-concept exploit that runs commands as root on "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener," with no credentials. Go programs open those listeners by default, per the Go Security Team. See the timeline. #Key facts FieldDetailCVECVE-2026-98432, "ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period," issued by the Linux kernel CNASeverityCritical, CVSS 3.1 9.8 (AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H), the kernel CNA's score. Red Hat also rates it Critical, CVSS 3.1 9.8, raised from Important (8.1) on October 30. Ubuntu rates it Critical, raised from High on November 3. SUSE rates it important, and Oracle and Amazon rate it Important with CVSS 3.1 8.1.WeaknessUse-after-free of IPv4 option data during the TCP handshake (the record lists no CWE)ImpactPer the CNA's scoring notes: kernel heap contents disclosed to the remote peer, kernel memory corruption, or a crash. Red Hat's bulletin: a remote, unauthenticated attacker "could exploit a race condition during TCP connection request processing to trigger remote code execution."Fixed in7.2.10 and 6.18.56 (Oct 11) · 6.12.113, 6.6.159, 6.1.190, 5.15.223, and 5.10.272 (Oct 15) · 7.3 (Oct 18)No fix yetUbuntu 16.04 through 26.04, as of 3:15 PM CST, November 3; fixes for 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04 are in testing. Red Hat still lists OpenShift's RHEL CoreOS and a separate RHEL 9 real-time kernel package as affected. Upstream branches that reached end-of-life before 5.10 get no fix.Proof of conceptAnthropic says Claude built a remote root exploit for servers with a multipath TCP listener. It hasn't published the exploit.CVE recordsPublished on cve.org on October 15. NVD lists it as "Received," with no analysis of its own, as of 3:15 PM CST, November 3.CreditReported by Xinyang Ge of Anthropic. Fixed by Eric Dumazet and reviewed by Kuniyuki Iwashima, per the fix commit. #Who is affected Any Linux kernel from 4.4 on that lacks the fix, whether it serves the network directly or hosts containers: a container runs on the host's kernel, so a new image doesn't change anything. IPv6 connections aren't affected by the main issue; the commit says "IPv6 is not affected by the first issue." As of 3:15 PM CST, November 3:

Ubuntu: rated Critical since November 3, raised from High. Fixed kernels for 22.04, 24.04, and 26.04 (5.15.0-203.213, 6.8.0-149.149, and 7.0.0-43.43) have been in its -proposed pocket, where Ubuntu tests updates before release, since October 26 and 27. Canonical's blog says it's testing them on "more than 2,000 certified servers and devices" before moving them to the updates pocket, and that users "who run their own kernel acceptance tests can choose to apply them" now; the post gives the steps. It lists 26.10 as "Fixed in 7.3.0-10.10," a kernel rebased on Linux 7.3 that has been in 26.10's updates pocket since October 28, and 16.04, 18.04, and 20.04, whose kernels now come through Ubuntu Pro, as "Fix pending." The tracker still lists the linux package as "Vulnerable" on every release, adding "work in progress" in those versions on 26.10 through 22.04. Many cloud and hardware-enablement kernels are listed the same way, and no Ubuntu Security Notice has been published. Red Hat: rated Critical, CVSS 3.1 9.8, since October 30. Fixed kernels shipped on November 1 for RHEL 8.10 (kernel-4.18.0-553.182.1.el8_10, RHSA-2026:93414, and its real-time kernel, RHSA-2026:93415), RHEL 9.8 (kernel-5.14.0-687.64.1.el9_8, RHSA-2026:93412), and RHEL 10.2 (kernel-6.12.0-211.72.1.el10_2, RHSA-2026:93413). The RHEL 9 and 10 updates include their real-time kernels. RHEL for NVIDIA was fixed on November 2 (RHSA-2026:93775), and the extended-support streams for RHEL 8.4 (RHSA-2026:94623), 8.8 (RHSA-2026:94303), 9.2 (RHSA-2026:94477, and its real-time kernel, RHSA-2026:94558), 9.4 (RHSA-2026:94109), 9.6 (RHSA-2026:94438), and 10.0 (RHSA-2026:94508) followed on November 2 and 3. OpenShift Container Platform 4 and 5, through RHEL CoreOS, are still listed as affected, as is a separate RHEL 9 kernel-rt package; RHEL 6 and 7 aren't affected (CVE page). Its bulletin, RHSB-2026-016, gives an nftables mitigation (compared below) and says any product that relies on the RHEL kernel "is also potentially impacted." For OpenShift, Red Hat says it "is preparing guidance," and warns that the nftables rule on a node doesn't filter traffic inside the cluster's network, "including pod to pod traffic." AlmaLinux: fixed kernels for AlmaLinux 8, 9, and 10 reached its production repositories early on November 2: kernel-4.18.0-553.182.1.el8_10, kernel-5.14.0-687.64.1.el9_8, and kernel-6.12.0-211.72.1.el10_2, the same versions as RHEL's (announcement). Its errata list them for AlmaLinux 8 (ALSA-2026:93414, and ALSA-2026:93415 for the real-time kernel) but not yet for 9 or 10. The kernels it put in its testing repository on October 30 also carry the fix. Debian: fixed in 12 "bookworm" (6.1.190-1, DLA-4841-1, and linux-6.12 6.12.113-1~deb12u1, DLA-4850-1), 13 "trixie" (6.12.113-1, DSA-6568-1), and unstable (tracker). SUSE: rated important. SUSE Linux Enterprise Server 16.0 (kernel-default 6.12.0-160000.40.1), 15 SP7 (6.4.0-150700.53.90.1), and the 15 SP4, SP5, and SP6 LTSS kernels are fixed; 15 SP7's real-time kernel is in progress. openSUSE Leap 16.0 is fixed, and Leap 15.6 is listed as affected (CVE page). Oracle Linux: rated Important, CVSS 3.1 8.1. Unbreakable Enterprise Kernel (UEK) errata for Oracle Linux 7, 8, 9, and 10 came out October 16: ELSA-2026-500397, ELSA-2026-500398, and ELSA-2026-500399 (CVE page). On November 2, Oracle added its Red Hat Compatible Kernel for Oracle Linux 8 (kernel-4.18.0-553.182.1.el8_10, ELSA-2026-93414), 9 (kernel-5.14.0-687.64.1.el9_8, ELSA-2026-93412), and 10 (kernel-6.12.0-211.72.1.el10_2, ELSA-2026-93413). Amazon Linux: rated Important, CVSS 3.1 8.1, and every kernel is fixed. On Amazon Linux 2023, the default kernel (ALAS2023-2026-3365, October 30), kernel6.12 (ALAS2023-2026-3335, October 29), and kernel6.18 (ALAS2023-2026-3251, October 24). On Amazon Linux 2, the core kernel (ALAS2-2026-4065) and the 5.4, 5.10, and 5.15 Extras kernels (ALAS2KERNEL-5.4-2026-135, ALAS2KERNEL-5.10-2026-137, and ALAS2KERNEL-5.15-2026-120), all October 30 (CVE page). AWS's bulletin adds that Amazon Linux 2023 instances locked to a release version need release 2023.12.20261102 or later, and that EKS-optimized Amazon Linux 2023 AMIs from release v20261031 and ECS-optimized AMIs from release 20261031 carry the fix.

#How the vulnerability works When a Linux server accepts a TCP connection, the kernel tracks the half-open handshake in a lightweight "request socket," then creates a full socket once the handshake completes. If the connecting peer's IPv4 header carried options, the kernel keeps them to echo in its replies. The bug: the kernel handed those saved options from the request socket to the new connection without copying them, then freed them immediately when the connection went away, while another CPU could still be reading them to build a handshake reply. Reading freed kernel memory is a use-after-free. The peer needs no login, and it all happens inside the kernel's handshake handling, before any application code runs. The CNA's scoring notes say the stale data can leak kernel heap memory back to the peer, steer kernel writes out of bounds, or crash the machine. Anthropic says a lost race "only fails the handshake without crashing the whole system, so a determined attacker can retry indefinitely until they succeed." #The fix Eric Dumazet's commit, "ipv4: free inet_opt and ireq_opt after an RCU grace period," changes two plain kfree() calls to kfree_rcu(), which waits until every reader has finished with the memory before freeing it. Other code paths that replace these options already did that. The commit also fixes the same problem in request-socket migration (net.ipv4.tcp_migrate_req=1, or a BPF_SK_REUSEPORT_SELECT_OR_MIGRATE program), and says a related IPv6 case "will be addressed in a separate patch." torvalds/linux · e3f33b0 · Oct 1, 2026net/ipv4/af_inet.c1 lines added, 1 removednet/ipv4/tcp_ipv4.c1 lines added, 1 removed2 files changed2 lines added, 2 removed #Which servers are exposed

Every Linux host that accepts IPv4 TCP connections on an affected kernel: web servers, SSH, databases, load balancers, and Kubernetes nodes. The CNA's notes say the vulnerable path runs "during the TCP handshake, before application authentication." Hosts with a multipath TCP (MPTCP) listener first. That's the setup Anthropic's working exploit needs: "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener." Anthropic hasn't said why that listener matters, and the CVE record doesn't mention MPTCP. A server has one only if an application opens an MPTCP socket, and Go programs do by default: the Go Security Team says "as of Go 1.24, Go programs enable MPTCP by default for listen sockets on Linux." The default follows the go line in the program's go.mod, and applies only where the kernel allows MPTCP (net.mptcp.enabled = 1, as on the Debian 12 kernel we checked; AlmaLinux says it ships MPTCP off). The Go team adds that "the underlying bug is not specific to MPTCP. It is possible that systems with no MPTCP listeners are vulnerable to similar attacks." The check is below. Hosts behind a pass-through load balancer. AWS's bulletin says its Network Load Balancer TCP listeners "pass client packets, including IP options, to targets," and tells customers to patch the Linux hosts behind them, and behind Global Accelerator, PrivateLink endpoint services, and VPC Lattice TCP listeners. Behind Application Load Balancer, CloudFront, or API Gateway, it says, customers "do not receive TCP connections from untrusted sources directly when following best practices."

children.author: gerdesj
children.textRawHtml:
Quite, however it looks quite rare:

"Why it's urgent: the bug sits in code every Linux server runs when it accepts an IPv4 TCP connection, before any application sees the connection. Anthropic, whose researcher reported it, says its Claude model wrote a working proof-of-concept exploit that runs commands as root on "Linux servers with a multipath TCP listener," with no credentials. Go programs open those listeners by default, per the Go Security Team. See the timeline."

I don't know of any Linux boxes running a multipath TCP listener in my care and I have quite a few. MP generally implies a router of some sort and the intersections in a Venn diagram continue to get smaller ...

This is still an issue and must be patched but I think it will be rare, very rare.

children.author: reissbaker
children.textRawHtml:
This is not rare. Every TCP connection in Go by default enables MPTCP [1]. Simply running a Go program that uses TCP without explicitly disabling this behavior will cause the running kernel to be vulnerable.

1: https://groups.google.com/g/golang-announce/c/PCoQcdxoScw

children.author: Eueudhsbsj32
children.textRawHtml: But any sane configuration would have the MPTCP port blocked behind a firewall (unless you were intentionally using MPTCP).
children.textZhHtml: But any sane configuration would have the MPTCP port blocked behind a firewall (unless you were intentionally using MPTCP).

children.author: hnlmorg
children.textRawHtml:
> MPTCP port blocked

MPTCP doesn’t use any specific ports. It’s an OSI layer higher than that. It’s part of the TCP protocol itself. So if your firewall routes TCP traffic of a specific port (eg HTTP) already then it’ll route MPTCP along with it too.

children.author: ButlerianJihad
children.textRawHtml: MPTCP is a protocol extension that requires cooperation by both peers and all middleboxes. So, if there is a Layer 7 firewall, or DPI/SPI, or TLS termination on the path, and it's not inclined to preserve the MPTCP options, then MPTCP will be disabled.
children.textZhHtml: MPTCP is a protocol extension that requires cooperation by both peers and all middleboxes. So, if there is a Layer 7 firewall, or DPI/SPI, or TLS termination on the path, and it's not inclined to preserve the MPTCP options, then MPTCP will be disabled.

children.author: hnlmorg
children.textRawHtml:
Firewalls do not operate at layer 7 nor do TLS termination.

What you’re thinking of is load balancers. Most of them will do TLS termination. But there’s also plenty of load balancing solutions out there that will forward the raw TCP traffic (AWS NLB, DNS based solutions, and so forth).

But it’s also worth noting that this vulnerability doesn’t explicitly need MPTCP. Just the POC exploit uses that.
